transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because I don’t really trust myself right now. Not in the sense that I’m trying to do something, but more like I feel like I’m this danger walking around, especially at work. There was this near-miss, and I keep replaying it over and over, and it’s like my brain has decided that it proves something about me — that I’m not meant to be a nurse, that I shouldn’t be around patients, that I’m a disappointment to everyone who believed in me.

And I know people might say, you know, “near-misses happen” or “that’s why there are systems,” but I can’t make myself believe that. I just keep thinking if I were better, more careful, more deserving, it wouldn’t have happened at all. It feels like I fooled everyone into thinking I could do this job, and now it’s obvious I can’t.

I feel like I’ve let everyone down. My patients, my coworkers, my family… even just being here, I feel embarrassed saying it out loud. But I can’t stop thinking that maybe everyone would be better off if I just wasn’t part of things, if I wasn’t in the way or capable of messing something up. That’s kind of why I came. I don’t know what to do with that feeling anymore.
Are you thinking about killing yourself right now?

I… I don’t have a plan. I’m not sitting here with some specific way I’m going to hurt myself, and I don’t think I’m about to leave here and do something. But I keep having these thoughts, and they scare me because they feel like they keep getting louder when I’m alone.

It’s more like… I’ll think, “It would be easier if I just didn’t wake up,” or “What if I could just disappear?” Not even in a dramatic way, just like… if I wasn’t here, then I couldn’t mess anything up again. I couldn’t hurt anyone, I couldn’t disappoint anyone, I couldn’t be this burden people have to deal with.

So I don’t know if that counts as thinking about killing myself exactly, but I am thinking about not being here. A lot. And I feel ashamed saying that, because part of me knows how it sounds, but that’s what’s been happening.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day?

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s there almost as soon as I wake up, this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, like before I even remember what I’m supposed to do that day, my body already feels sad.

And then I try to go to work and act normal, because I have to. I’ll be smiling at patients, talking to them in Spanish, trying to sound warm and steady and like I’m fully there with them… and inside I feel like I’m barely holding myself together. It’s like I’m performing being okay, and I can do it for little stretches, but the feeling doesn’t really go away. It just sits underneath everything.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I have. I used to have little things that helped me feel like myself, even if my day was bad. Like jogging — I’d go for a run and it would kind of clear my head, like at least my body was doing something and I could breathe for a while. Or I’d knit, which sounds kind of old-lady-ish, I know, but it used to calm me down because it was repetitive and I could make something. I liked cooking too, and reading after class when I still had the energy for it.

Now I just… don’t care. I’ll come home and sit on my bed still in my scrubs, and I’ll look at my running shoes or my knitting stuff or a book sitting there, and I know those are things I used to want to do. I know they’re supposed to help. But I can’t make myself reach for them. It feels like there’s no point, or like it would take too much effort to even pretend I’d enjoy it.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Just change clothes, just cook something, just read one page,” and then I just sit there. And then time passes, and I’m still sitting there in the same clothes, not doing anything. It’s like the part of me that used to care about those things just shut off.
How long have you been feeling this depressed most days?

It’s been… a long time. I think about a year and a couple months now. Like maybe around fourteen months.

It started after I graduated high school and then went straight into taking college classes and working full-time at the clinic. At first I told myself it was just stress, like I was adjusting and being dramatic or tired because everything changed so fast. But it didn’t really lift. It just kind of became the way most days felt, and then I realized months were going by and I was still waking up feeling like this.

So… yeah, about a year and two months, I’d say. Since that transition after graduation.
Have you noticed a change in your appetite?

Yeah… it’s changed. I don’t really feel hungry the way I used to, or I guess I don’t notice it. A lot of days I’ll get all the way to late afternoon or even evening and realize I haven’t actually eaten anything real. Like I’ll have coffee, maybe, and then I just keep going, and it doesn’t occur to me until I feel kind of shaky or my stomach feels weird.

And then when I do notice, it’s not like I want a meal. I’ll sort of force myself to eat something small, like crackers or whatever is easy, just because I know I’m supposed to put something in my body. But it feels more like a chore than hunger.

I’ve noticed my work pants are getting loose too, which is… I don’t know, it makes me feel a little uneasy because I’m not trying to lose weight. I’m not dieting or anything. I just forget to eat, and then when I remember, I don’t really want much.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yeah… sleep has been bad. I don’t know if it’s that I can’t sleep at all, exactly, but it’s like my brain won’t shut off when I’m trying to.

I’ll get into bed and I’ll be exhausted, like physically tired, and then the second it’s quiet I start replaying everything from work. Charts, whether I documented something right, medication calculations, little things someone said, whether I forgot to double-check something. It’s not even always one clear mistake I’m worried about — it’s more like my brain keeps searching for one. I’ll be lying there thinking through doses or trying to remember if I signed something off, and then I check the time and it’s way later than I thought.

And then when I finally do fall asleep, it doesn’t feel restful. I wake up before my alarm a lot, already tense, already exhausted, like I’m starting the day behind. Sometimes the first feeling I have when I wake up is this scared feeling, like, “Did I miss something?” before I’m even fully awake. So even if I technically slept for some amount of time, it doesn’t feel like I actually rested.
Have other people noticed that you’re moving or talking more slowly than usual?

Yeah… a little. I didn’t notice it at first, or I kind of didn’t want to notice it, but people at the clinic have said things.

Like someone will ask if I’m tired, not in a mean way, just like, “Are you okay? You seem really tired today.” And I think part of it is because I’m slower getting things, like if I’m grabbing supplies or restocking something, it takes me longer than it should. I’ll be standing there looking at the shelf like I know what I came for, but my body just feels delayed or something.

And with talking too… sometimes someone asks me a simple question, something I should answer immediately, and there’s this pause before I can get the words out. It’s only a few seconds, but I can feel it happening, and then I get embarrassed because I know they’re waiting. It makes me seem like I’m not paying attention, but I am. It’s just slower.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yeah… definitely. That’s actually been one of the things that scares me the most, because it’s not just like I’m distracted for a minute. It feels like my brain gets foggy, like I’m looking right at something and it’s not going in.

At work, I’ll read a medication order and then realize I have to read it again… and then again, because I don’t trust that I actually understood it the first time. It’s like my eyes move over the words, but my brain doesn’t hold onto them. And then I get stuck checking myself, because obviously with meds I can’t just be “kind of sure.” So something that should be quick takes me way longer.

It happens with school stuff too. I’ll look at a lecture slide and read the same line over and over, and I know it’s basic information I should be able to process, but it just feels like there’s a delay. Like everything has to pass through mud before I understand it.

Even small choices feel harder than they should. Like deciding what to chart first, or what task to do next, I’ll just freeze for a second and kind of stare at the screen. It’s embarrassing because I know I’m capable of doing these things, but lately it feels like my brain won’t organize itself.
Have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

Yeah… I have. That’s honestly a big part of why I came in, because I can’t seem to get away from this feeling that I’m… dangerous, I guess. Like not dangerous on purpose, but like I’m someone who could hurt a patient because I’m not careful enough or good enough or stable enough to be doing this.

There was that near-miss, and I know people can say, “It didn’t happen,” or “It was caught,” or whatever, but in my head it doesn’t feel small. It feels like proof. Like proof that I’m not meant to be a nurse, and that everyone who believed I could do this was wrong. I keep replaying it and thinking, if I was better, if I was sharper, if I was the kind of person who should be trusted with patients, it wouldn’t have happened at all.

And then it turns into this bigger thing, where I feel like I’m disappointing everyone — my coworkers, my family, my instructors, patients who need someone competent. I feel like I’m taking up space in a role I don’t deserve. Sometimes it feels like everyone would be better off without me there, because then at least they wouldn’t have to worry about whether I’m going to mess something up.
When you feel like you're a danger to patients, have you ever heard a voice or had a fixed belief that others couldn't talk you out of telling you that you’ve harmed someone or deserve punishment?

I mean… not like a voice, no. It’s not like I hear someone outside of me saying it, or like there’s a message telling me I have to be punished. It’s more… it’s my own thoughts, but they get really stuck and loud in my head.

Like I can know, technically, that the near-miss was caught and that people have told me it doesn’t mean I’m a horrible nurse or that I’m unsafe forever. I can hear that, and part of me understands what they’re saying. But emotionally it still feels like proof that I shouldn’t be trusted. Like if I were really meant to do this, if I were actually competent, then it wouldn’t have happened at all.

So I wouldn’t say nobody could talk me out of it completely, because I do have moments where I can kind of see the logical side. But the feeling comes right back — that I’m a danger, that I’m disappointing everyone, that patients would be better off if I wasn’t the one taking care of them. It’s not a fixed belief like I literally know I harmed someone. It’s more this constant guilt that I can’t shake.
Have you ever had a period of several days or longer when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or very irritable?

I don’t think so… not for several days or anything like that.

I mean, I get irritable sometimes, but it doesn’t feel unusual in that way you’re describing. It’s more like I’m overwhelmed or tired and then I’m short with people, and afterward I usually feel bad about it. I can’t really think of a time where I was suddenly feeling amazing or euphoric, like I had all this energy or confidence for days.

If anything, when I’ve had “better” moments, they’re pretty brief — like maybe I get through a shift or I have a couple hours where I feel a little more normal, and then it fades. But I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch of several days where I felt high or unusually up. And the irritability doesn’t feel like a separate episode, if that makes sense.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy nearly every day?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean… I feel tired a lot, but I don’t know if it’s “unusually” tired or nearly every day in the way you mean.

Some days I feel kind of drained, but I’ve also been trying to tell myself that’s just because work is demanding and I’m probably not handling everything well. So it’s hard for me to separate what’s normal tired from something else. I haven’t really been tracking it. Like, I know there are times where I don’t feel like I have much energy, but I don’t know if I can honestly say it’s every day or that it’s noticeably different enough.

I guess I’d say I’ve noticed feeling worn down, but I’m not totally sure how much.
Have these symptoms made it hard for you to function at work, in school, or at home?

Yeah… I think it has. I don’t really like admitting that, because part of me wants to say I’m still managing, like I’m still showing up and trying to keep everything together. But it’s definitely made things harder.

With school, I’ve fallen behind in my nursing prerequisites. Not in a dramatic “I quit everything” way, but enough that I’m behind on assignments and studying, and then the more behind I get, the harder it is to start again. I’ll sit there knowing I need to do it, and then I just feel stuck and guilty because I’m not keeping up the way I should.

And at work, I’m functioning, but not the way I used to. I’ve been asking coworkers to double-check things that I used to do confidently without even thinking twice. Like tasks that should feel normal for me now suddenly feel risky, and I need someone else to confirm I’m not missing something. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I don’t want them to think I can’t do my job.

It’s made me afraid to take on normal clinic responsibilities. Even when something is part of my role, I second-guess myself so much that I hesitate or try to get reassurance first. So yes… it’s affecting work and school, and probably home too in the sense that I bring all of that stress back with me.
Even on days when nothing stressful happens at work, do you still feel depressed most of the day?

Yeah… I think so. Even when nothing specific happens at work, it’s still there.

Most days I wake up already feeling like there’s this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, if that makes sense. It’s not always tied to something that happened that day. Sometimes I’ll get to the clinic and everything is technically fine — no one’s upset with me, patients are normal, the day isn’t even that stressful — but I still feel like I’m carrying something around inside me.

And I can smile at patients, especially when I’m speaking Spanish with them or trying to be warm and normal, and from the outside I probably look okay. But inside I feel like I’m just barely holding myself together. Like I’m performing being fine, and then as soon as there’s a quiet moment, that heaviness is still there. So… yes, it’s not only on bad workdays. It’s most days.
Do these feelings seem much stronger than you’d expect just from the work incident and stress?

Yeah… I think they do. I keep trying to tell myself this is just normal stress after what happened, like anyone would feel shaken up after a near-miss at work, but it feels bigger than that now.

It’s not just, “I made a mistake and I need to be more careful.” It turns into this whole thing in my head where I feel like I’m a danger to people, like that one incident proves something awful about me as a person. Like maybe I’m not meant to be a nurse at all, and I fooled myself into thinking I could do this.

And I know that probably sounds dramatic, because nothing terrible actually happened, but it doesn’t feel that way inside. It feels like proof that I’m careless or unsafe or… I don’t know, a disappointment. Like I’m letting down my coworkers, my patients, my family, everyone who thought I could handle this.

That’s honestly a big part of why I came in. I can’t stop feeling like everyone would be better off if I just wasn’t there in that role, because then I couldn’t mess something up or hurt someone. It feels much stronger than just “work was stressful.” It feels like I’m the problem.
Over the past six months, have you found yourself worrying excessively about many different things, not just work?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean… I do worry a lot, but when I think about it, it feels mostly tied back to work and whether I’m messing things up or falling behind.

I don’t know if I’d say it’s been “many different things” across the board for six months. Like, I’m not constantly worrying about every possible area of my life in the same way. It’s more like one main thread that spreads into other things because I’m already stressed, if that makes sense.

So… maybe some, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed excessive worry about lots of unrelated things. It feels more centered around what’s been happening with work and school.
Have you been having repeated thoughts that you would be better off dead?

Yeah… I have. I feel really ashamed saying that out loud, but yes.

It’s not like I have a plan to hurt myself or anything specific like that. I don’t have some method picked out, and I’m not sitting there making arrangements. But I keep having these thoughts where I just think… it would be easier if I didn’t wake up. Or if I could just disappear for a while, or disappear completely, so I wouldn’t have to keep feeling like this and I wouldn’t be able to mess anything up again.

It’s more like I get overwhelmed and my brain goes to, “Everyone would be safer or better off if I just wasn’t here,” which scares me because I don’t really want to say that, and I don’t want to worry people. But the thought keeps coming back, especially when I feel like I’ve failed or like I’m going to hurt someone by making another mistake.

So… yes, I’ve been having thoughts like that. Not a plan, but thoughts that maybe it would be easier if I just didn’t exist.
Before this started about fourteen months ago, was there a period of at least two months when your mood felt mostly normal?

I’m trying to think back clearly… but no, I don’t think there was really a solid two-month stretch where I felt mostly normal once this started.

It’s been going on for about a year and two months now, I think. It started around the time after I graduated high school and began college classes and full-time clinic work. At first I told myself it was just because everything changed all at once, like I was adjusting to being out of high school and suddenly having all these responsibilities. But it didn’t really lift in a clear way.

There may have been better days, or maybe a week here and there where I could function more normally, but not two months where I’d say, “Yeah, I felt like myself again.” It’s more like it’s been this ongoing thing since then.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop feeling like I'm a danger and a disappointment, like that one near-miss proves I'm not meant to be a nurse and everyone would be better off without me.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so the chief complaint symptom code must be returned.

patient.answer:

There was this near-miss, and I keep replaying it over and over, and it’s like my brain has decided that it proves something about me — that I’m not meant to be a nurse, that I shouldn’t be around patients, that I’m a disappointment to everyone who believed in me.

And I know people might say, you know, “near-misses happen” or “that’s why there are systems,” but I can’t make myself believe that. But I can’t stop thinking that maybe everyone would be better off if I just wasn’t part of things, if I wasn’t in the way or capable of messing something up. That’s kind of why I came. I don’t know what to do with that feeling anymore.

doctor.question: Are you thinking about killing yourself right now?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I don't have a plan to hurt myself, but I keep having thoughts like it would be easier if I didn't wake up or if I could just disappear so I wouldn't mess anything up again.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about current suicidal intent, which falls under recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t have a plan. I’m not sitting here with some specific way I’m going to hurt myself, and I don’t think I’m about to leave here and do something. But I keep having these thoughts, and they scare me because they feel like they keep getting louder when I’m alone.

It’s more like… I’ll think, “It would be easier if I just didn’t wake up,” or “What if I could just disappear?” Not even in a dramatic way, just like… if I wasn’t here, then I couldn’t mess anything up again. I couldn’t hurt anyone, I couldn’t disappoint anyone, I couldn’t be this burden people have to deal with.

So I don’t know if that counts as thinking about killing myself exactly, but I am thinking about not being here. A lot. And I feel ashamed saying that, because part of me knows how it sounds, but that’s what’s been happening.

doctor.question: Have you been feeling depressed most of the day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, and even when I'm smiling at patients in Spanish or trying to act normal at the clinic, I feel like I'm just barely holding myself together.

patient.answer:
Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s there almost as soon as I wake up, this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, like before I even remember what I’m supposed to do that day, my body already feels sad.

And then I try to go to work and act normal, because I have to. I’ll be smiling at patients, talking to them in Spanish, trying to sound warm and steady and like I’m fully there with them… and inside I feel like I’m barely holding myself together. It’s like I’m performing being okay, and I can do it for little stretches, but the feeling doesn’t really go away. It just sits underneath everything.

doctor.intent: Assess severity by determining whether there is marked loss of interest or pleasure, which helps distinguish major depressive episode from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or burnout.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to clear my head by jogging, knitting, cooking, or reading after class, but now I just sit on my bed in my scrubs and can't make myself care about any of it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities, which matches Loss_of_Interest.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. I used to have little things that helped me feel like myself, even if my day was bad. Like jogging — I’d go for a run and it would kind of clear my head, like at least my body was doing something and I could breathe for a while. Or I’d knit, which sounds kind of old-lady-ish, I know, but it used to calm me down because it was repetitive and I could make something. I liked cooking too, and reading after class when I still had the energy for it.

Now I just… don’t care. I’ll come home and sit on my bed still in my scrubs, and I’ll look at my running shoes or my knitting stuff or a book sitting there, and I know those are things I used to want to do. I know they’re supposed to help. But I can’t make myself reach for them. It feels like there’s no point, or like it would take too much effort to even pretend I’d enjoy it.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Just change clothes, just cook something, just read one page,” and then I just sit there. And then time passes, and I’m still sitting there in the same clothes, not doing anything. It’s like the part of me that used to care about those things just shut off.

inference.note: Current turn adds clear anhedonia, which strengthens a depressive episode over anxiety/adjustment/burnout, but does not yet establish severity, duration, or fully rule out alternatives.

doctor.intent: Assess duration of the depressive episode to distinguish major depressive episode from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or burnout.
doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this depressed most days?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a year and two months, starting after I graduated high school and began college classes and full-time clinic work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the depressed mood has been present most days, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
It’s been… a long time. I think about a year and a couple months now. Like maybe around fourteen months.

It started after I graduated high school and then went straight into taking college classes and working full-time at the clinic. At first I told myself it was just stress, like I was adjusting and being dramatic or tired because everything changed so fast. But it didn’t really lift. It just kind of became the way most days felt, and then I realized months were going by and I was still waking up feeling like this.

So… yeah, about a year and two months, I’d say. Since that transition after graduation.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the depression is pervasive beyond the work-related trigger by checking for appetite disturbance, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment-related distress or burnout.
doctor.question: Have you noticed a change in your appetite?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: I forget to eat until late in the day, then I might force down crackers or coffee, and my work pants have been getting loose even though I'm not trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about changes in appetite, which matches the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it’s changed. I don’t really feel hungry the way I used to, or I guess I don’t notice it. A lot of days I’ll get all the way to late afternoon or even evening and realize I haven’t actually eaten anything real. Like I’ll have coffee, maybe, and then I just keep going, and it doesn’t occur to me until I feel kind of shaky or my stomach feels weird.

And then when I do notice, it’s not like I want a meal. I’ll sort of force myself to eat something small, like crackers or whatever is easy, just because I know I’m supposed to put something in my body. But it feels more like a chore than hunger.

I’ve noticed my work pants are getting loose too, which is… I don’t know, it makes me feel a little uneasy because I’m not trying to lose weight. I’m not dieting or anything. I just forget to eat, and then when I remember, I don’t really want much.

doctor.intent: Assess insomnia or hypersomnia as a core depressive symptom to help distinguish major depressive episode severity from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or burnout.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble sleeping?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: At night I lie there replaying charts and medication calculations, and when I do fall asleep I wake up before my alarm already exhausted and scared I missed something.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about trouble sleeping, which matches the sleep disturbance symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… sleep has been bad. I don’t know if it’s that I can’t sleep at all, exactly, but it’s like my brain won’t shut off when I’m trying to.

I’ll get into bed and I’ll be exhausted, like physically tired, and then the second it’s quiet I start replaying everything from work. Charts, whether I documented something right, medication calculations, little things someone said, whether I forgot to double-check something. It’s not even always one clear mistake I’m worried about — it’s more like my brain keeps searching for one. I’ll be lying there thinking through doses or trying to remember if I signed something off, and then I check the time and it’s way later than I thought.

And then when I finally do fall asleep, it doesn’t feel restful. I wake up before my alarm a lot, already tense, already exhausted, like I’m starting the day behind. Sometimes the first feeling I have when I wake up is this scared feeling, like, “Did I miss something?” before I’m even fully awake. So even if I technically slept for some amount of time, it doesn’t feel like I actually rested.

doctor.intent: Assess psychomotor change to help gauge major depressive episode severity and distinguish depressive disorder from anxiety/adjustment/burnout.
doctor.question: Have other people noticed that you’re moving or talking more slowly than usual?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: People at the clinic have asked if I'm tired because I move slower getting supplies and sometimes it takes me a few seconds to answer even simple questions.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether others have noticed slowed movement or speech, which directly matches observable psychomotor slowing.

patient.answer:
Yeah… a little. I didn’t notice it at first, or I kind of didn’t want to notice it, but people at the clinic have said things.

Like someone will ask if I’m tired, not in a mean way, just like, “Are you okay? You seem really tired today.” And I think part of it is because I’m slower getting things, like if I’m grabbing supplies or restocking something, it takes me longer than it should. I’ll be standing there looking at the shelf like I know what I came for, but my body just feels delayed or something.

And with talking too… sometimes someone asks me a simple question, something I should answer immediately, and there’s this pause before I can get the words out. It’s only a few seconds, but I can feel it happening, and then I get embarrassed because I know they’re waiting. It makes me seem like I’m not paying attention, but I am. It’s just slower.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the depression includes impaired concentration/indecisiveness to help determine severity between moderate and severe major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble concentrating?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: I have to read the same medication order or lecture slide over and over because my brain feels foggy, and even small choices like what to chart first can freeze me up.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about trouble concentrating, which matches diminished ability to think or concentrate.

patient.answer:
Yeah… definitely. That’s actually been one of the things that scares me the most, because it’s not just like I’m distracted for a minute. It feels like my brain gets foggy, like I’m looking right at something and it’s not going in.

At work, I’ll read a medication order and then realize I have to read it again… and then again, because I don’t trust that I actually understood it the first time. It’s like my eyes move over the words, but my brain doesn’t hold onto them. And then I get stuck checking myself, because obviously with meds I can’t just be “kind of sure.” So something that should be quick takes me way longer.

It happens with school stuff too. I’ll look at a lecture slide and read the same line over and over, and I know it’s basic information I should be able to process, but it just feels like there’s a delay. Like everything has to pass through mud before I understand it.

Even small choices feel harder than they should. Like deciding what to chart first, or what task to do next, I’ll just freeze for a second and kind of stare at the screen. It’s embarrassing because I know I’m capable of doing these things, but lately it feels like my brain won’t organize itself.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has excessive guilt or feelings of worthlessness, which would help confirm a major depressive episode and distinguish severity from anxiety/stress-related conditions.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop feeling like I'm a danger and a disappointment, like that one near-miss proves I'm not meant to be a nurse and everyone would be better off without me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. That’s honestly a big part of why I came in, because I can’t seem to get away from this feeling that I’m… dangerous, I guess. Like not dangerous on purpose, but like I’m someone who could hurt a patient because I’m not careful enough or good enough or stable enough to be doing this.

There was that near-miss, and I know people can say, “It didn’t happen,” or “It was caught,” or whatever, but in my head it doesn’t feel small. It feels like proof. Like proof that I’m not meant to be a nurse, and that everyone who believed I could do this was wrong. I keep replaying it and thinking, if I was better, if I was sharper, if I was the kind of person who should be trusted with patients, it wouldn’t have happened at all.

And then it turns into this bigger thing, where I feel like I’m disappointing everyone — my coworkers, my family, my instructors, patients who need someone competent. I feel like I’m taking up space in a role I don’t deserve. Sometimes it feels like everyone would be better off without me there, because then at least they wouldn’t have to worry about whether I’m going to mess something up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode is severe by assessing psychotic features, which would separate major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or burnout and clarify between moderate and severe depression.
doctor.question: When you feel like you're a danger to patients, have you ever heard a voice or had a fixed belief that others couldn't talk you out of telling you that you’ve harmed someone or deserve punishment?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop feeling like I'm a danger and a disappointment, like that one near-miss proves I'm not meant to be a nurse and everyone would be better off without me.
target_item.reason: The question is directly assessing whether her guilt and belief that she is dangerous to patients has become delusional or involved voices, which falls under worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt.

patient.answer:
I mean… not like a voice, no. It’s not like I hear someone outside of me saying it, or like there’s a message telling me I have to be punished. It’s more… it’s my own thoughts, but they get really stuck and loud in my head.

Like I can know, technically, that the near-miss was caught and that people have told me it doesn’t mean I’m a horrible nurse or that I’m unsafe forever. I can hear that, and part of me understands what they’re saying. But emotionally it still feels like proof that I shouldn’t be trusted. Like if I were really meant to do this, if I were actually competent, then it wouldn’t have happened at all.

So I wouldn’t say nobody could talk me out of it completely, because I do have moments where I can kind of see the logical side. But the feeling comes right back — that I’m a danger, that I’m disappointing everyone, that patients would be better off if I wasn’t the one taking care of them. It’s not a fixed belief like I literally know I harmed someone. It’s more this constant guilt that I can’t shake.

inference.note: Denied hallucinations and delusional conviction; guilt appears mood-congruent rather than psychotic, supporting nonpsychotic depressive episode and not changing the candidate list.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood suggesting bipolar spectrum illness rather than unipolar depression or anxiety-related conditions.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of several days or longer when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or very irritable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about possible manic or hypomanic episodes, which are not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not for several days or anything like that.

I mean, I get irritable sometimes, but it doesn’t feel unusual in that way you’re describing. It’s more like I’m overwhelmed or tired and then I’m short with people, and afterward I usually feel bad about it. I can’t really think of a time where I was suddenly feeling amazing or euphoric, like I had all this energy or confidence for days.

If anything, when I’ve had “better” moments, they’re pretty brief — like maybe I get through a shift or I have a couple hours where I feel a little more normal, and then it fades. But I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch of several days where I felt high or unusually up. And the irritability doesn’t feel like a separate episode, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Assess for fatigue or loss of energy as a remaining major depressive symptom to help distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, or burnout.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or low energy nearly every day, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific fatigue/energy symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean… I feel tired a lot, but I don’t know if it’s “unusually” tired or nearly every day in the way you mean.

Some days I feel kind of drained, but I’ve also been trying to tell myself that’s just because work is demanding and I’m probably not handling everything well. So it’s hard for me to separate what’s normal tired from something else. I haven’t really been tracking it. Like, I know there are times where I don’t feel like I have much energy, but I don’t know if I can honestly say it’s every day or that it’s noticeably different enough.

I guess I’d say I’ve noticed feeling worn down, but I’m not totally sure how much.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are causing clinically significant impairment in functioning, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from subthreshold depression, adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety, or burnout.
doctor.question: Have these symptoms made it hard for you to function at work, in school, or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve fallen behind in my nursing prerequisites and at work I’ve needed coworkers to double-check tasks I used to handle confidently, which makes me afraid to take on normal clinic responsibilities.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the symptoms have interfered with functioning at work, school, or home.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think it has. I don’t really like admitting that, because part of me wants to say I’m still managing, like I’m still showing up and trying to keep everything together. But it’s definitely made things harder.

With school, I’ve fallen behind in my nursing prerequisites. Not in a dramatic “I quit everything” way, but enough that I’m behind on assignments and studying, and then the more behind I get, the harder it is to start again. I’ll sit there knowing I need to do it, and then I just feel stuck and guilty because I’m not keeping up the way I should.

And at work, I’m functioning, but not the way I used to. I’ve been asking coworkers to double-check things that I used to do confidently without even thinking twice. Like tasks that should feel normal for me now suddenly feel risky, and I need someone else to confirm I’m not missing something. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I don’t want them to think I can’t do my job.

It’s made me afraid to take on normal clinic responsibilities. Even when something is part of my role, I second-guess myself so much that I hesitate or try to get reassurance first. So yes… it’s affecting work and school, and probably home too in the sense that I bring all of that stress back with me.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the depressive symptoms are tied specifically to the identifiable stressor at work or are pervasive beyond it, to distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder and burnout.
doctor.question: Even on days when nothing stressful happens at work, do you still feel depressed most of the day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, and even when I'm smiling at patients in Spanish or trying to act normal at the clinic, I feel like I'm just barely holding myself together.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether a depressed mood persists most of the day even without an immediate work stressor.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Even when nothing specific happens at work, it’s still there.

Most days I wake up already feeling like there’s this heavy, empty feeling in my chest, if that makes sense. It’s not always tied to something that happened that day. Sometimes I’ll get to the clinic and everything is technically fine — no one’s upset with me, patients are normal, the day isn’t even that stressful — but I still feel like I’m carrying something around inside me.

And I can smile at patients, especially when I’m speaking Spanish with them or trying to be warm and normal, and from the outside I probably look okay. But inside I feel like I’m just barely holding myself together. Like I’m performing being fine, and then as soon as there’s a quiet moment, that heaviness is still there. So… yes, it’s not only on bad workdays. It’s most days.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the depressive syndrome is clearly out of proportion to the identifiable stressor, helping distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder and burnout.
doctor.question: Do these feelings seem much stronger than you’d expect just from the work incident and stress?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop feeling like I'm a danger and a disappointment, like that one near-miss proves I'm not meant to be a nurse and everyone would be better off without me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the patient’s guilt and self-blame feel excessive or disproportionate compared with the work incident and stress.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think they do. I keep trying to tell myself this is just normal stress after what happened, like anyone would feel shaken up after a near-miss at work, but it feels bigger than that now.

It’s not just, “I made a mistake and I need to be more careful.” It turns into this whole thing in my head where I feel like I’m a danger to people, like that one incident proves something awful about me as a person. Like maybe I’m not meant to be a nurse at all, and I fooled myself into thinking I could do this.

And I know that probably sounds dramatic, because nothing terrible actually happened, but it doesn’t feel that way inside. It feels like proof that I’m careless or unsafe or… I don’t know, a disappointment. Like I’m letting down my coworkers, my patients, my family, everyone who thought I could handle this.

That’s honestly a big part of why I came in. I can’t stop feeling like everyone would be better off if I just wasn’t there in that role, because then I couldn’t mess something up or hurt someone. It feels much stronger than just “work was stressful.” It feels like I’m the problem.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has pervasive anxiety and worry across multiple areas of life, which would help distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from a major depressive episode or adjustment-related condition.
doctor.question: Over the past six months, have you found yourself worrying excessively about many different things, not just work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry across many different areas over the past six months, which is more directly related to generalized anxiety symptoms. The provided symptom profile does not include an item for excessive worry or anxiety beyond work.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean… I do worry a lot, but when I think about it, it feels mostly tied back to work and whether I’m messing things up or falling behind.

I don’t know if I’d say it’s been “many different things” across the board for six months. Like, I’m not constantly worrying about every possible area of my life in the same way. It’s more like one main thread that spreads into other things because I’m already stressed, if that makes sense.

So… maybe some, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed excessive worry about lots of unrelated things. It feels more centered around what’s been happening with work and school.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there is recurrent passive suicidal ideation, which is a key major depressive episode criterion and helps distinguish severe from moderate depression among the current candidates.
doctor.question: Have you been having repeated thoughts that you would be better off dead?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I don't have a plan to hurt myself, but I keep having thoughts like it would be easier if I didn't wake up or if I could just disappear so I wouldn't mess anything up again.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about repeated thoughts of being better off dead, which matches recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. I feel really ashamed saying that out loud, but yes.

It’s not like I have a plan to hurt myself or anything specific like that. I don’t have some method picked out, and I’m not sitting there making arrangements. But I keep having these thoughts where I just think… it would be easier if I didn’t wake up. Or if I could just disappear for a while, or disappear completely, so I wouldn’t have to keep feeling like this and I wouldn’t be able to mess anything up again.

It’s more like I get overwhelmed and my brain goes to, “Everyone would be safer or better off if I just wasn’t here,” which scares me because I don’t really want to say that, and I don’t want to worry people. But the thought keeps coming back, especially when I feel like I’ve failed or like I’m going to hurt someone by making another mistake.

So… yes, I’ve been having thoughts like that. Not a plan, but thoughts that maybe it would be easier if I just didn’t exist.

doctor.intent: Determine whether her depressive symptoms are episodic versus chronic/persistent to distinguish major depressive episode from burnout or adjustment-related symptoms.
doctor.question: Before this started about fourteen months ago, was there a period of at least two months when your mood felt mostly normal?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a year and two months, starting after I graduated high school and began college classes and full-time clinic work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the time course of symptoms and whether there was a sustained normal-mood interval before the current 14-month episode.

patient.answer:
I’m trying to think back clearly… but no, I don’t think there was really a solid two-month stretch where I felt mostly normal once this started.

It’s been going on for about a year and two months now, I think. It started around the time after I graduated high school and began college classes and full-time clinic work. At first I told myself it was just because everything changed all at once, like I was adjusting to being out of high school and suddenly having all these responsibilities. But it didn’t really lift in a clear way.

There may have been better days, or maybe a week here and there where I could function more normally, but not two months where I’d say, “Yeah, I felt like myself again.” It’s more like it’s been this ongoing thing since then.

inference.note: Sustained depressed mood and anhedonia for ~14 months with no 2-month return to baseline, plus appetite/weight loss, insomnia, psychomotor slowing, poor concentration, excessive guilt/worthlessness, functional impairment, and recurrent thoughts of death strongly support a current major depressive episode. Psychosis and bipolarity were not supported. Adjustment disorder, GAD, and burnout are less likely given severity, breadth of neurovegetative symptoms, suicidality, and persistence beyond a stress reaction.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms: persistent depressed mood and markedly diminished interest for about 14 months, along with appetite/weight loss, insomnia, psychomotor slowing, impaired concentration, excessive guilt/worthlessness, recurrent thoughts of death, and clear functional impairment in work and school. Severity is supported by pervasive suicidal ideation and extensive impairment. Psychotic features were specifically probed and denied.
